title: Transactional Sagas
subtitle: Read the eight combinations before choosing one
summary: A transactional saga coordinates local changes across distributed services when one atomic database transaction is unavailable. The chapter analyzes eight combinations formed by three dimensions: synchronous or asynchronous communication, atomic or eventual consistency, and orchestrated or choreographed coordination. The familiar Epic Saga is synchronous, atomic, and orchestrated; it is easy to recognize but highly coupled and operationally constrained. Relaxing atomicity usually removes the hardest coordination problems. Asynchrony improves parallelism and responsiveness but introduces ordering, race, deadlock, queue, and recovery concerns. Choreography removes a mediator but distributes workflow state and compensation logic. The Parallel Saga offers a strong combination for complex workflows needing scale, while the Anthology Saga offers high throughput for simple workflows with infrequent errors. The names are a comparison aid; the dimensions and their consequences are the real design tool.

concepts.title: Eight combinations
concepts.body: Saga choices are a matrix, not a single recipe. Communication can be synchronous or asynchronous; consistency can be atomic or eventual; coordination can be orchestrated or choreographed. The eight named patterns make intersections discussable, and their superscripts encode the three selected dimensions. Changing one dimension changes the downstream trade-offs.
concepts.example: Epic is synchronous, atomic, orchestrated. Anthology is asynchronous, eventual, choreographed. Comparing their dimensions explains the behavior better than memorizing their literary names.

concepts.title: Epic Saga
concepts.body: The Epic Saga models monolithic transaction behavior with synchronous calls, atomic consistency, and an orchestrator. A failed final call triggers compensating updates to earlier services. Its mediator provides a clear owner and familiar semantics, but timing bottlenecks, database restrictions, failure modes, and low elasticity make distributed atomicity expensive.
concepts.example: An order mediator updates inventory and payment, then fails on shipping and asks the first two services to undo their writes.

concepts.title: Phone Tag
concepts.body: Phone Tag keeps atomic consistency and synchronous calls but replaces orchestration with choreography. The first service becomes a front controller and each service carries compensation logic. Happy paths can avoid a mediator bottleneck, yet complexity rises with workflow semantics and failure paths, so the pattern fits simple workflows.
concepts.example: A reservation service calls payment, which calls fulfillment; a failure sends synchronous compensating requests back along the chain.

concepts.title: Eventual consistency
concepts.body: Fairy Tale and Time Travel remove holistic atomicity and let each domain service own local transactionality. Fairy Tale retains synchronous orchestration and is comparatively simple. Time Travel uses synchronous choreography for one-way, high-throughput flows, but services must model errors and state themselves. Both trade immediate global agreement for more design freedom.
concepts.example: A mediator can cache a change while a down service recovers in Fairy Tale. A one-way ingestion chain can settle over time in Time Travel.

concepts.title: Asynchronous atomicity
concepts.body: Fantasy Fiction and Horror Story show why adding asynchrony while keeping atomicity is difficult. Pending workflows overlap, responses arrive out of order, and coordinators or services must track undo information, races, and dependencies. Horror Story combines those problems with choreography and is especially complex. Performance gains in isolation do not survive entangled constraints.
concepts.example: If workflow Gamma depends on pending Alpha while Beta also runs, an atomic asynchronous mediator must track all three states and their failure ordering.

concepts.title: Parallel Saga
concepts.body: Parallel Saga uses asynchronous communication, eventual consistency, and orchestration. The mediator coordinates requests and responses without a global transaction, allowing parallel execution and local scaling. It still must resolve retries, synchronization, and asynchronous error paths, but it is attractive for complex workflows that need throughput and a visible workflow owner.
concepts.example: A ticket mediator sends independent enrichment requests to several services and later issues retry or corrective messages for the ones that fail.

concepts.title: Anthology Saga
concepts.body: Anthology Saga combines asynchronous communication, eventual consistency, and choreography. It has the least coupling and supports high throughput because no mediator or holistic transaction blocks progress. In return, services carry workflow context, error handling, and eventual correction. It suits simple or infrequently failing flows; complex recovery can make its distributed logic hard to operate.
concepts.example: A stream of independent records moves through local consumers that retry their own failures and publish corrective events when needed.

concepts.title: State machines
concepts.body: When eventual consistency and errors matter, a saga state machine records the current state and drives retries or manual correction toward a valid outcome. State ownership is a coordination decision, not an implementation afterthought. The machine makes progress and recovery explicit even when updates occur in separate local transactions.
concepts.example: A ticket saga records NEW, PAYMENT_DONE, FULFILLMENT_PENDING, and COMPENSATING states, allowing a retry worker to resume from the recorded point.

misconceptions.claim: A saga pattern name guarantees a clean distributed transaction.
misconceptions.correction: A pattern names recurring forces and trade-offs. Distributed atomicity still has failure modes, compensation limits, and operational costs.

misconceptions.claim: Asynchronous communication automatically makes an atomic workflow scalable.
misconceptions.correction: Asynchrony adds parallelism but atomic coordination adds pending state, ordering, races, and recovery complexity. Eventual consistency is often the larger relaxation.

scenario.title: Process a high-volume order
scenario.context: A retailer must accept orders, reserve stock, authorize payment, and notify customers. Order volume is spiky, payment and stock services have different response times, and operators need to resume failed workflows. The business accepts a short period of eventual consistency if customers receive clear status. Choose a saga shape that matches complexity and throughput.

options.label: Parallel saga
options.benefit: Orchestration gives one workflow owner while asynchronous local transactions allow parallelism and independent scaling.
options.cost: The mediator and state machine must handle retries, timing, and corrective actions.
options.consequence: Stock and payment requests run concurrently. A payment timeout leaves a visible pending state and a retry path rather than blocking every other order in a global transaction.

options.label: Epic saga
options.benefit: Synchronous atomic behavior resembles the business’s familiar all-or-nothing transaction.
options.cost: A slow or unavailable participant blocks the mediator and compensation can be difficult and expensive.
options.consequence: The team gets immediate success or failure semantics, but peak traffic queues behind the coordinator and a shipping failure requires undoing earlier distributed writes.

scenario.debrief: The stated tolerance for eventual consistency and need for scale favor Parallel Saga. If legal or domain requirements truly demand atomic outcomes, the team must accept the corresponding coupling and test compensation boundaries.

quiz.question: Which dimensions define the saga matrix?
quiz.explanation: The chapter varies communication, consistency, and coordination to derive eight combinations.

quiz.question: Which pattern uses asynchronous communication and eventual consistency with orchestration?
quiz.explanation: Parallel Saga retains a mediator but relaxes synchronous and atomic constraints.

quiz.question: Why is a saga state machine useful?
options: It makes all services share one database
It records progress and supports retries or correction
It removes the need to model errors
quiz.explanation: The state machine makes eventual progress and recovery explicit; it does not remove distributed failure.

exercise.title: Score a saga matrix
exercise.prompt: For one workflow, write the communication, consistency, and coordination choice. Rate coupling, complexity, responsiveness, and scale, then describe one failure and its recovery state.

fields.label: Decision
fields.placeholder: Three saga dimensions and selected pattern

steps.text: Start one business workflow across service boundaries.
Select synchronous or asynchronous, atomic or eventual, and orchestration or choreography.
Execute local transactions and emit results or failures.
Record saga progress and pending work.
Retry, compensate, or route a durable correction.
